analysis.one_liner: Provides full public financing and stricter rules for Senate campaigns, including a soft money ban.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 4 Democratic cosponsors in June 1997 and referred to the Senate Rules Committee; no further action and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Senate candidates who collect a large number of small $5 contributions from voters in their state opt into full public funding of their campaigns, in exchange for agreeing to raise no private money. It would also ban national political parties from raising unlimited 'soft money', require broadcasters to give participating candidates free airtime at reduced rates, force disclosure of electioneering 'issue ads', restrict franked mass mailings in election years, and restructure the FEC. It never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who cannot afford to make large campaign contributions would gain a system in which Senate candidates are financed by small-dollar and public money rather than by wealthy donors and interest groups. Candidates without personal wealth or wealthy networks could run competitive campaigns. Taxpayers would also gain from the elimination of soft money and broader disclosure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters without large donations to give

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a 'clean money' system: a Senate candidate who collects enough small $5 qualifying contributions from state voters is certified and receives public campaign funds for the primary, general, and runoff elections.

Prohibits national party committees from soliciting or spending 'soft money' — contributions not subject to federal contribution limits and source prohibitions — and bars candidates and incumbents from raising such funds.
Entitles participating candidates to free broadcast time (30 minutes primary, 60 minutes general) in prime hours and caps their broadcast ad rates at half the lowest rate.

Requires disclosure of 'issue advertisements' naming a Senate candidate, tightens the definition of independent expenditures, and limits party committee spending in races with a clean money candidate.
Bars Members of Congress from sending franked (taxpayer-funded) mass mailings in their election year unless not running, restricting a common incumbent self-promotion tool.
Requires participating candidates to appear in at least one primary and two general election public debates, and mandates paid candidate ads carry an approval statement.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the Senate Election Fund, and broadcast stations would provide free airtime and reduced ad rates to participating candidates. Wealthy donors, big-money PACs, and party committees raising unlimited soft money would lose their access channels to Senate campaigns.

drawbacks.text: Public financing requires federal appropriations, so taxpayers would directly fund Senate campaigns, and the bill's stated intent to reduce government waste depends on contested behavioral assumptions.

Spending limits could disadvantage candidates facing heavily financed opponents, though the bill includes matching funds when a private-money opponent or independent spending exceeds 125% of the clean money amount, capped at 200%.
The free broadcast time and half-price ad mandates are unfunded requirements imposed on broadcasters, who could be expected to litigate or pass costs elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a comprehensive overhaul: public financing in exchange for private-money bans, a soft money prohibition, disclosure of issue ads, and FEC restructuring. Its benefits for ordinary voters are substantial and it imposes direct costs on big-money donors and party committees; the costs to taxpayers are real but modest relative to a federal budget, and its main cost is borne by wealthy donors and broadcasters rather than the public.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on introduction, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. John Kerry (D-MA) on June 17, 1997, with 4 Democratic cosponsors (Wellstone, Glenn, Biden, Leahy).
Read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration the day of introduction.
No further legislative action was recorded in the bill's action history before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy donors, special-interest PACs, and the national party committees that raise unlimited soft money were better off, since the campaign financing channels that give them access to senators remained untouched. Incumbents also retained the status quo, including franked mass mailings in election years.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors and party soft money

for.name: Sen. John F. Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act in the Senate on June 17, 1997 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: Sens. Paul Wellstone, John Glenn, Joseph Biden, and Patrick Leahy

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral at introduction and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting the bill die.

against.name: Republican Senate leadership
against.role: Held the chamber's agenda in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Declined to advance the bill or its comprehensive public-financing approach to the floor, though this bill never reached any vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five original sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the bill drew no Republican support in the record and never advanced in the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill bans national and congressional party committees from soliciting or spending unlimited, unregulated 'soft money', eliminating their most lucrative fundraising channel. State party committees would lose the ability to fundraise for tax-exempt organizations and face restrictions on spending unregulated money in federal election years.

Public financing plus matching funds remove the access that large campaign contributions currently buy in Senate races, and disclosure of issue ads exposes election-year spending by interest groups. These groups would lose a key lever of influence over senators.

Broadcast stations would be required to provide participating candidates free prime-time airtime and to sell additional time at 50% of the lowest rate, plus face preemption restrictions on candidate advertising. This cuts into ad revenue, though the same stations also profit from paid political advertising in elections generally.

industries.industry: Political consultants and campaign media firms
industries.note: Public funding would replace large-scale private ad buys in Senate races, shrinking the pool of big-money media contracts. At the same time, candidates who opted in would still spend public funds on professional campaign services.
The bill bans use of personal funds by participating candidates and caps spending, reducing the advantage of wealthy or self-financed Senate candidates.
